summary: Discovery focused on p95 latency targets and throughput. EchoWare needs sub-200ms p95 for short responses at ~40-80 concurrency and streaming support; exploring hosted trial then Dedicated for predictable SLOs, with Private (VPC) for data residency. Agreed to run a perf POC with Redwood harness and share security docs.
topics: dedicated vs hosted vs private tradeoffs
transcript:
[00:00] Ben Carter (AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining, i'm Ben from Redwood, i'm here with Sara and Mina from our solutions engineering team. how's everyone doin?
[00:06] Tom Ellis (EchoWare): Good thanks, Tom here. we wanted to dig into latency and throughput, p95 targets specifically. we run chat and short summarization in product.
[00:12] Priya Rao (EchoWare): hey, priya here, im the SRE, i'll focus on concurrency and our traffic profile.
[00:18] Ben Carter: Great, quick agenda — gather requirements, walk through what we recommend for hitting p95 targets at scale, and agree next steps.
[00:28] Sara Nguyen (SE): quick question about current stack — Tom, what models are you using today and where are they hosted?
[00:36] Tom Ellis: Mostly open models hosted on cloud endpoints, a mix of Mistral and Llama variants, some quantized. currently on GCP with autoscaling endpoints, but latency is inconsistent. p95 sits around 650-800ms right now for short responses, which is too high.
[00:52] Ben Carter: ok that makes sense. what are your target p95 numbers?
[00:56] Liam Chen (EchoWare): We want sub-200ms p95 for single-turn short chat messages (~20-40 tokens). For longer completions it's okay to be higher but baseline is 200ms.
[01:06] Sara Nguyen: got it. and what's typical concurrency? Priya?
[01:10] Priya Rao: steady-state concurrency is about 40-60 concurrent requests during peak, spikes up to 120 for events. median sequence length ~30 tokens, 95th ~120 tokens. We also rely on streaming for UI perceived latency.
[01:24] Mina Patel: Streaming changes the game; chunking vs server-side streaming, do you use SSE or websockets?
[01:29] Tom Ellis: currently websocket streaming. we need low tail latency per first token.
[01:34] Sara Nguyen: Okay, so two performance goals: p95 first-token ~200ms and sustain tokens/sec at scale. A few notes: hosted Redwood can hit great numbers for bursts and early testing, Dedicated gives you predictable GPU pools which make p95 much more consistent. Private/VPC is for compliance but same stack.
[01:52] Priya Rao: curious about what hardware you use for Dedicated.
[01:54] Mina Patel: we run a mix — customer options include reserved A100/H100 nodes depending on availability and model. kernel selection and compilation path matter a lot; our runtime tunes kernels for your sequence length distribution.
[02:08] Ben Carter: also continuous batching, KV cache and prefix caching can reduce cost and improve tail. but batching increases latency if not tuned.
[02:15] Tom Ellis: about batching — our UX needs first token quickly; we can't buffer too long. how do you approach that?
[02:22] Sara Nguyen: we do dynamic batching with latency SLO knobs — you can configure max batch wait (e.g., 2–10ms) and max batch size. for first-token sensitive work we prioritize low-wait policies and route to smaller pools.
[02:34] Priya Rao: what's realistic p95 with a single H100 for 20-40 token responses?
[02:40] Mina Patel: rough numbers: with optimized kernels and quantized 4-bit model variants you can see p95 in the 80–180ms range for those short responses at low-medium concurrency. on A100 numbers can be higher, around 120–260ms depending on variants. these are ballpark, we need to bench with your exact model and token distribution.
[02:58] Tom Ellis: we do care about token/sec for longer runs. how do you measure throughput?
[03:03] Sara Nguyen: we measure tokens/sec for steady-state generation, plus p95 for first token and 95th for end-to-end response. our perf harness will run generated prompts at your concurrency and measure token/sec, p50/p95/p99 latencies.
[03:15] Ben Carter: important to note streaming adds overhead per token, so we measure streaming token throughput separately from non-streaming single-call throughput.
[03:22] Tom Ellis: can you run benchmarks that mimic websocket streaming with 30-token bursts?
[03:26] Sara Nguyen: yes, that's part of the POC plan — we'll provide k6 + websocket scripts to simulate the streaming and token cadence.
[03:33] Priya Rao: and what about KV cache/long context? we maintain user convo history ~4k tokens sometimes.
[03:39] Mina Patel: KV cache is handled in the runtime; cache hits vastly reduce latency because you avoid recalc for prefixes. for 4k contexts we manage KV in memory and we have memory-compute tradeoffs. large contexts can hurt throughput but caching previous tokens helps.
[03:51] Tom Ellis: any gotchas around quantization vs quality? we care about generation quality for summarization.
[03:56] Sara Nguyen: quantization can be model-dependent; we recommend doing A/B evals. Redwood Optimize can suggest quant profiles per workload; typically for chat short responses 4-bit QLoRA-style runs well but we should run your eval set.
[04:10] Ben Carter: security and compliance — you mentioned options earlier?
[04:14] Liam Chen: yes our security team requires SOC2, SSO via SAML, audit logs, and KMS integration for key management. also some data residency constraints in EU.
[04:23] Mina Patel: Redwood supports SOC2, SAML SSO, RBAC, and integrates with customer KMS for Private deployments; hosted customers can use our managed encryption with options for customer-managed keys. we'll attach our security pack.
[04:36] Priya Rao: great. on the topic of fallbacks — if a dedicated pool is saturated do you have graceful degradation?
[04:42] Sara Nguyen: yes, smart routing routes to compatible model variants or fall back to hosted pool with agreed SLA and cost penalty. we can also configure circuit breakers and queueing policies.
[04:52] Tom Ellis: ok can you outline the POC we just discussed?
[04:55] Ben Carter: POC plan: 1) Redwood runs bench with your model (or a close open model) using your traffic profile, measure p95 first-token and tokens/sec; 2) test streaming via websocket scripts; 3) run Dedicated prototype with reserved nodes to validate tail stability; 4) deliver benchmark spreadsheet and recommendations.
[05:14] Priya Rao: timeline? we want a result in two weeks ideally.
[05:17] Sara Nguyen: we can get initial harness and run in ~4 business days once we get traffic profile and sample prompts. Dedicated prototype may take a week to provision depending on region.
[05:27] Tom Ellis: is there any cost estimate for a week-long dedicated prototype?
[05:31] Ben Carter: we'll include a cost estimate in the TCO doc — short answer: prototype is typically a small reserved pool (2–4 GPUs) for a week and is modest, we'll send numbers.
[05:40] Priya Rao: about monitoring, we need token-level cost and latency breakdowns and traces when things spike.
[05:45] Mina Patel: Redwood Console has per-route token/latency breakdown, traces, and alerting. we'll show a demo in the follow-up.
[05:52] Tom Ellis: any specific logs we should expect for debugging timeouts?
[05:55] Sara Nguyen: you get request traces with model variant, queue time, batch size, kernel path, and per-token generation durations. that helps root cause p95 spikes.
[06:06] Ben Carter: alright, next steps recap — we'll share the benchmark harness, dedicated pricing, security docs, and set up the POC next Tue. Priya to send traffic profile and sample prompts.
[06:17] Priya Rao: will do.
[06:19] Tom Ellis: one more question — do you support automatic quantization tuning or do we manage that?
[06:23] Mina Patel: Redwood Optimize can recommend quantization profiles; our SEs can run automated quantization sweeps and report quality/regression metrics.
[06:32] Ben Carter: perfect. thanks everyone. we'll follow up with the docs.
[06:36] [call ends]

Note: transcript contains occasional mis-hearings (e.g., "key cache" vs "KV cache") and minor punctuation artifacts consistent with auto-generated call transcripts.
